what_its_for: Metolazone is a water pill (diuretic) that helps your body get rid of extra salt and water through your urine. It is used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and swelling (edema) caused by heart failure, kidney disease, or liver disease. By removing extra fluid, it helps lower blood pressure and reduce swelling in your legs, ankles, or feet.
how_to_take: Take metolazone exactly as your doctor prescribes. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. You can take it with or without food, but taking it with food may help prevent an upset stomach. Try to take it at the same time each day. Because this medicine makes you urinate more, it is best to take it in the morning so it does not disturb your sleep at night. Do not stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first, even if you feel well.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your condition. The usual dose ranges from 2.5 mg to 20 mg once daily, but your dose may be different. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions. Do not take more or less than prescribed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still the same day. If it is already the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store metolazone at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it in a dry place, away from moisture and heat. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use the medicine after the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking metolazone, as it can increase dizziness and lower blood pressure too much. Be careful when standing up quickly from sitting or lying down, as this medicine can cause dizziness or lightheadedness. Avoid getting too hot or becoming dehydrated — drink enough fluids unless your doctor tells you to limit fluids. Avoid taking extra potassium supplements or salt substitutes without asking your doctor first. Tell your doctor or pharmacist before taking any new medicines, including over-the-counter pain relievers like ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) or naproxen (Aleve), as they can reduce how well metolazone works.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency help if you experience: severe dizziness or fainting, muscle cramps, weakness, or irregular heartbeat (these may be signs of low potassium or other electrolyte problems), signs of dehydration such as extreme thirst, dry mouth, or urinating very little, signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, itching, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing, unusual bleeding or bruising, yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), sudden vision changes, or severe nausea and vomiting. Also call your doctor if your swelling or blood pressure is not improving.
when_it_works: You may notice that you urinate more frequently within the first few hours of taking metolazone. For swelling (edema), you may start to see improvement within a few days. For high blood pressure, it may take a few weeks of regular use before you feel the full benefit. Even if you feel fine, keep taking the medicine as prescribed.
special_populations: Older adults (seniors): You may be more sensitive to the effects of this medicine, especially dizziness, low blood pressure, and electrolyte changes. Use extra caution when standing up to avoid falls. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor before using this medicine if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Breastfeeding: It is not known if metolazone passes into breast milk. Discuss the risks and benefits with your doctor before breastfeeding. Kidney or liver disease: Your doctor will monitor you more closely, as this medicine can affect how well your kidneys and liver work. Children: Safety and dosing in children has not been well established; use only under close medical supervision.
